---
title: "Forest Bill, 1910"
subtitle: "The First Major Attempt to Centralize Forest Control"
---


The Forest Bill of 1911 marked a turning point. It proposed a more centralized system for forest reservation and forest management. Its stated aim was to provide for the establishment, conservation, and management of forest reserves; to allow the reservation, acquisition, or relinquishing of land or rights over land by government; and to regulate the taking, collection, sale, purchase, possession, and export of forest produce.

African critics immediately recognized the danger. The bill gave the colonial government power not only over land but also over the products of the forest. Forests were not simply timber stands. They were sources of fuelwood, medicine, hunting, farming land, sacred power, and community livelihood. By regulating forest produce and access, the bill threatened everyday practices as well as customary authority.

Casely Hayford and other critics treated the bill as part of a longer history of colonial land encroachment. They compared it to earlier land legislation, especially the Crown Lands Bills. Chiefs and educated elites argued that the bill would deprive communities of land and then punish them for using places they had historically owned. One criticism focused on penalties that could include fines or imprisonment for entering or using reserved land without official consent.

The 1911 bill failed because African leaders saw it as too direct an assault on customary land rights. Yet it was not forgotten. It became the legal and political rehearsal for the Forest Ordinance of 1927. Many of the ideas that appeared in 1911 returned later in revised form.
